facts.statement: Stegoceras lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 77.5 to 74 million years ago.
facts.quote: Stegoceras is a genus of pachycephalosaurid (dome-headed) dinosaur that lived in what is now North America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 77.5 to 74 million years ago (mya).

facts.statement: The first specimens of Stegoceras were described in 1902 from Alberta, Canada, establishing the type species Stegoceras validum.
facts.quote: The first specimens from Alberta, Canada, were described in 1902, and the type species Stegoceras validum was based on these remains.

facts.statement: The name Stegoceras means "horn roof" and the specific name validum means "strong".
facts.quote: The generic name means "horn roof", and the specific name means "strong".

facts.statement: Stegoceras was a small, bipedal dinosaur measuring 2 to 2.5 meters in length and weighing between 10 and 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: Stegoceras was a small, bipedal dinosaur about 2 to 2.5 m long, and weighed around 10 to 40 kg.

facts.statement: Stegoceras had a roughly triangular skull with a short snout and a thick, broad, relatively smooth dome on top.
facts.quote: The skull was roughly triangular with a short snout, and had a thick, broad, and relatively smooth dome on the top.

facts.statement: Researchers believe Stegoceras skulls were flat in juveniles and developed into domes as the animals aged.
facts.quote: The skull is thought to have been flat in juvenile animals and to have grown into a dome with age.

facts.statement: Stegoceras was likely a herbivore with a good sense of smell.
facts.quote: Stegoceras was most likely herbivorous, and it probably had a good sense of smell.

facts.statement: The function of the Stegoceras dome is debated, with theories ranging from combat and sexual display to species recognition.
facts.quote: The function of the dome has been debated, and competing theories include use in intra-specific combat (head or flank-butting), sexual display, or species recognition.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe collected the first known remains of Stegoceras from the Belly River Group in Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: The first known remains of Stegoceras were collected by palaeontologist Lawrence Lambe from the Belly River Group, in the Red Deer River district of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe named the genus and species Stegoceras validus in 1902 based on initial specimens.
facts.quote: Based on these specimens, Lambe described and named the new monotypic genus and species Stegoceras validus in 1902.

facts.statement: John Bell Hatcher designated specimen CMN 515 as the lectotype for Stegoceras validum in 1907.
facts.quote: Because the species was based on multiple specimens (a syntype series), CMN 515 was designated as the lectotype specimen by palaeontologist John Bell Hatcher in 1907.

facts.statement: Franz Nopcsa suggested in 1903 that the domes were frontal and nasal bones forming a single unpaired horn.
facts.quote: In 1903, palaeontologist Franz Nopcsa von Felső-Szilvás suggested that the fragmentary domes of Stegoceras were in fact frontal and nasal bones, and that the animal would therefore have had a single, unpaired horn.

facts.statement: In 1918, Lambe named the species S. brevis based on specimen CMN 1423, which he had previously included in S. validus.
facts.quote: In 1918, Lambe assigned another dome (CMN 138) to S. validus, and named a new species, S. brevis, based on specimen CMN 1423 (which he originally included in S. validus).

facts.statement: Nopcsa doubted the association of the skull and skeleton, suggesting the skull belonged to a nodosaur and the skeleton to an ornithopod.
facts.quote: Because the skull seemed so specialized compared to the rather "primitive"-looking skeleton, Nopcsa doubted whether these parts actually belonged together, and suggested the skull belonged to a nodosaur, the skeleton to an ornithopod, and the supposed gastralia (belly ribs) to a fish.

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg demonstrated dental differences in 1945, suggesting Troodon was a theropod and dome-headed dinosaurs formed their own family.
facts.quote: In 1945, after examining casts of T. formosus and S. validus teeth, palaeontologist Charles M. Sternberg demonstrated differences between the two, and instead suggested that Troodon was a theropod dinosaur, and that the dome-headed dinosaurs should be placed in their own family.

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurs, including Stegoceras, are grouped with horned ceratopsians in the clade Marginocephalia.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurs are today grouped with the horned ceratopsians in the group Marginocephalia.

facts.statement: Stegoceras is considered a basal or primitive member of the pachycephalosaur family.
facts.quote: Stegoceras itself has been considered basal (or "primitive") compared to other pachycephalosaurs.

facts.statement: S. validum fossils are found in the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations, while S. novomexicanum is found in the Fruitland and Kirtland Formations.
facts.quote: S. validum is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation and the Oldman Formation, whereas S. novomexicanum is known from the Fruitland and Kirtland Formation.

facts.statement: The species S. novomexicanum is debated and may not belong to the genus Stegoceras.
facts.quote: The remaining assigned species, S. novomexicanum, named in 2011 from fossils found in New Mexico, has also been debated, and may not belong to Stegoceras.

facts.statement: The specific name of S. browni honors Brown, who discovered the holotype specimen AMNH 5450 in Alberta.
facts.quote: The specific name honours Brown, who found the holotype specimen (specimen AMNH 5450 in the American Museum of Natural History) in Alberta.

facts.statement: In 1983, Galton and Hans-Dieter Sues reclassified S. browni into the genus Ornatotholus, viewing it as the first known American "flat-headed" pachycephalosaur.
facts.quote: In 1983, Galton and Hans-Dieter Sues moved S. browni to its own genus, Ornatotholus (ornatus is Latin for "adorned" and tholus for "dome"), and considered it the first known American member of a group of "flat-headed" pachycephalosaurs, previously known from Asia.

facts.statement: In 2000, Robert M. Sullivan moved several species to the genus Prenocephale and considered S. bexelli a dubious name because its holotype was incomplete and possibly lost.
facts.quote: In 2000, palaeontologist Robert M. Sullivan assigned S. edmontonensis and S. brevis to the genus Prenocephale (until then only known from the Mongolian species P. prenes), and found it more likely that S. bexelli belonged to Prenocephale than to Stegoceras, but considered it a nomen dubium (dubious name, without distinguishing characters) due to its incompleteness, and noted its holotype specimen appeared to be lost.

facts.statement: In 2003, Williamson and Carr debated whether Ornatotholus was a dubious name or simply a juvenile Stegoceras.
facts.quote: In 2003, Thomas E. Williamson and Thomas Carr considered Ornatotholus a nomen dubium, or perhaps a juvenile Stegoceras.

facts.statement: In 2003, Robert M. Sullivan synonymized Ornatotholus with Stegoceras and created the new genera Colepiocephale and Hanssuesia for other species.
facts.quote: In a 2003 revision of Stegoceras, Sullivan agreed that Ornatotholus was a junior synonym of Stegoceras, moved S. lambei to the new genus Colepiocephale, and S. sternbergi to the new genus Hanssuesia, named after Sues.

facts.statement: The specimen UALVP 2 remains the most complete Stegoceras known and forms the basis for most scientific understanding of the genus.
facts.quote: UALVP 2 is still the most complete specimen of Stegoceras, upon which most scientific understanding of the genus is based.

facts.statement: In 2016 and 2021, researchers moved S. brevis to the genus Foraminacephale and S. bexelli to the genus Sinocephale.
facts.quote: S. brevis was moved to the new genus Foraminacephale in 2016 by Ryan K. Schott Schott and David C. Evans, and S. bexelli to Sinocephale in 2021 by Evans and colleagues.

facts.statement: In 2023, Aaron D. Dyer and colleagues used synchrotron data to find no significant differences between Gravitholus and Hanssuesia skulls and those of S. validum.
facts.quote: In 2023, palaeontologist Aaron D. Dyer and colleagues analysed sutures and individual elements in the skulls of Gravitholus and Hanssuesia, the former based on synchrotron data, and found no significant distinction between them and Stegoceras validum.

facts.statement: Dyer and colleagues considered Gravitholus and Hanssuesia to be juvenile stages of Stegoceras, with Gravitholus representing the end of growth.
facts.quote: They considered both as junior synonyms, with Gravitholus representing the end-stage in the growth of Stegoceras.

facts.statement: In 2002, Williamson and Carr described a dome from New Mexico as a juvenile pachycephalosaur of uncertain species, possibly Sphaerotholus goodwini.
facts.quote: In 2002, Williamson and Carr described a dome (specimen NMMNH P-33983 in the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science) from the San Juan Basin, New Mexico, which they considered a juvenile pachycephalosaur of uncertain species (though perhaps Sphaerotholus goodwini).

facts.statement: In 2006, Sullivan and Spencer G. Lucas identified the New Mexico dome as a juvenile S. validum, suggesting a much wider range for the species.
facts.quote: In 2006, Sullivan and Spencer G. Lucas considered it a juvenile S. validum, which would expand the range of the species considerably.

facts.statement: In 2011, Jasinski and Sullivan reclassified the New Mexico dome as an adult and named it the holotype of the new species Stegoceras novomexicanum.
facts.quote: In 2011, palaeontologist Steven E. Jasinski and Sullivan considered the specimen an adult, and made it the holotype of the new species Stegoceras novomexicanum, with two other specimens (SMP VP-2555 and SMP VP-2790) as paratypes.

facts.statement: In 2016, Williamson and Stephen L. Brusatte found that the paratypes of S. novomexicanum did not match the holotype and that all specimens were juveniles.
facts.quote: In 2016, palaeontologists Williamson and Stephen L. Brusatte restudied the holotype of S. novomexicanum and found that the paratypes did not belong to the same taxon as the holotype, and that all the involved specimens were juveniles.

facts.statement: In 2024, Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman described a juvenile Stegoceras specimen from the Aguja Formation of Texas.
facts.quote: In 2024, a specimen of Stegoceras from the Aguja Formation of Texas was described, and assigned to Stegoceras based on morphometric analyses by palaeontologists Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman.

facts.statement: Stegoceras was estimated to be about 2 to 2.5 meters long, roughly the size of a goat.
facts.quote: Its length is estimated to have been about 2 to 2.5 m, comparable to the size of a goat.

facts.statement: The weight of Stegoceras has been estimated to range from 10 to 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: The weight has been estimated to be about 10 to 40 kg.

facts.statement: Stegoceras was considered small to medium-sized compared to other pachycephalosaurs.
facts.quote: Stegoceras was small to medium in size compared to other pachycephalosaurs.

facts.statement: It is debated whether S. novomexicanum was smaller than S. validum, as the status of its known specimens as adults or juveniles remains uncertain.
facts.quote: S. novomexicanum appears to have been smaller than S. validum, but it is disputed whether the known specimens (incomplete skulls) are adults or juveniles.

facts.statement: The frontoparietal dome was broad with a relatively smooth surface, except for wrinkled sides.
facts.quote: The frontoparietal dome was broad and had a relatively smooth surface, with only the sides being rugose (wrinkled).

facts.statement: Much of the skull, except the upper dome surface, was ornamented with nodes arranged in rows.
facts.quote: Except for the upper surface of the dome, much of the skull was ornamented with nodes, many arranged in rows.

facts.statement: Stegoceras possessed differentiated teeth that were set in sockets.
facts.quote: Stegoceras had teeth that were heterodont (differentiated) and thecodont (placed in sockets).

facts.statement: The front edges of the tooth crowns bore eight denticles, while the back edge bore nine to eleven.
facts.quote: The front edges of the crowns bore eight denticles (serrations), and the back edge bore nine to eleven.

facts.statement: Like other pachycephalosaurs, Stegoceras would have had a small beak.
facts.quote: Like other pachycephalosaurs, it would have had a small beak.

facts.statement: Stegoceras is distinct for its lack of nasal ornamentation and a reduced gap between the front teeth.
facts.quote: It is also distinct in its lack of nasal ornamentation, and in having a reduced diastema.

facts.statement: The vertebral column was very rigid due to articulations that prevented sideways movement and was strengthened by ossified tendons.
facts.quote: The articulation between the zygagophyses (articular processes) of successive dorsal (back) vertebrae appears to have prevented sideways movement of the vertebral column, which made it very rigid, and it was further strengthened by ossified tendons.

facts.statement: The tail contained unique myorhabdoi structures found only in pachycephalosaurs among four-limbed animals, which may have stiffened the tail.
facts.quote: Such structures are called myorhabdoi, and are otherwise only known in teleost fish; the feature is unique to pachycephalosaurs among tetrapod (four-limbed) animals, and may have functioned in stiffening the tail.

facts.statement: The shoulder blade was longer than the upper arm bone, slender, narrow, and slightly twisted.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) was longer than the humerus (upper arm bone); its blade was slender and narrow, and slightly twisted, following the contour of the ribs.

facts.statement: Stegoceras likely had five-fingered hands and four toes, similar to other pachycephalosaurs.
facts.quote: Though the limbs of Stegoceras are not completely known, they were most likely like other pachycephalosaurs in having five-fingered hands and four toes.

facts.statement: In 1978, Stegoceras was placed in the family Pachycephalosauridae by Dong Zhiming.
facts.quote: In 1978, the Chinese palaeontologist Dong Zhiming split Pachycephalosauria into two families; the dome-headed Pachycephalosauridae (including Stegoceras) and the flat-headed Homalocephalidae

facts.statement: In 1986, Paul Sereno grouped Stegoceras with ceratopsians in the suborder Marginocephalia based on skull features.
facts.quote: In 1986, palaeontologist Paul Sereno supported the relationship between pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians, and united them in the group Marginocephalia

facts.statement: In 2003, researchers determined that Stegoceras is more primitive than fully-domed pachycephalosaurs.
facts.quote: In 2003, Sullivan found Stegoceras itself to be more basal (or "primitive") than the "fully-domed" members of the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae

facts.statement: It is debated whether the flat-headed condition in some pachycephalosaurs represents a juvenile trait or an advanced derived feature rather than sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: The dome-headed/flat-headed division of the pachycephalosaurs was abandoned in the following years, as flat heads were considered paedomorphic (juvenile-like) or derived ("advanced") traits in most revisions, but not a sexually dimorphic trait

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Schott and colleagues placed Stegoceras within the family Pachycephalosauridae.
facts.quote: The cladogram below shows the placement of Stegoceras within Pachycephalosauridae according to Schott and colleagues, 2016:

facts.statement: In 2021, researchers found that Stegoceras teeth were statistically distinct from those of Thescelosaurus despite both having heterodont dentition.
facts.quote: In 2021, palaeontologist Michael N. Hudgins and colleagues examined the teeth of Stegoceras and Thescelosaurus and found that while both had heterodont teeth, they could be statistically distinguished from each other

facts.statement: In 2026, researchers found that the skull dome of Stegoceras limited jaw muscle movement and constrained its feeding style.
facts.quote: In 2026, palaeontologists Louis-Philippe Bateman and Hans C.E. Larsson examined the feeding performance in pachycephalosaurs using Stegoceras as a model, and found that the presence of their domes limited the space and movement of their jaw muscles

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that the skull dome of Stegoceras constrained its evolution to an ancestral, low-fiber herbivorous diet and may have been a social display structure.
facts.quote: They concluded that the dome constrained pachycephalosaurs to a more plesiomorphic (ancestral) dentition with a low-fiber herbivorous niche, and that it was an example of a sociosecual display structure constraining evolution of feeding traits

facts.statement: In 2014, Jason M. Bourke and colleagues proposed that Stegoceras possessed cartilaginous nasal turbinates to direct airflow to its olfactory region.
facts.quote: In 2014, Jason M. Bourke and colleagues found that Stegoceras would have needed cartilaginous nasal turbinates in the front of the nasal passages for airflow to reach the olfactory region

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that nasal turbinates in Stegoceras helped cool arterial blood flowing to the brain.
facts.quote: The blood vessel system in the passages also suggest that the turbinates served to cool down warm arterial blood from the body that was heading to the brain

facts.statement: The oldest known pachycephalosaurs, such as Acrotholus, lived about 84 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The oldest known members of the group (such as Acrotholus) are "fully domed" and known from the Santonian stage of the Late Cretaceous period (about 84 million years ago)

facts.statement: Stegoceras lived about 77 million years ago during the Middle Campanian stage.
facts.quote: This is before the supposedly more primitive Stegoceras from the Middle Campanian (77 million years ago) and Homalocephale from the Early Maastrichtian (70 million years ago)

facts.statement: Pachycephalosaurs, including Stegoceras, are found in both North America and Asia.
facts.quote: Pachycephalosaurs appear abruptly in the fossil record, and are present in both North America and Asia

facts.statement: Researchers Brown and Schlaikjer hypothesized that the variation in dome size represented sexual dimorphism, with flat-headed specimens being female Stegoceras.
facts.quote: Brown and Schlaikjer suggested that there was sexual dimorphism in the degree of doming, and hypothesized that flat-headed specimens such as AMNH 5450 (Ornatotholus) represented the female morph of Stegoceras.

facts.statement: Williamson and Carr (2003) proposed a growth series where Ornatotholus represented the juvenile stage of Stegoceras validum.
facts.quote: In 2003, Williamson and Carr published a hypothetical growth series of S. validum, showing Ornatotholus as the juvenile stage.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Schott and colleagues found that ornamentation on the parietosquamosal shelf remained consistent during growth while vascularity in the domes decreased as size increased.
facts.quote: In 2011, Schott and colleagues made a more comprehensive analysis of cranial dome ontogeny in S. validum. The study found that the parietosquamosal shelf conserved the arrangement of ornamentation throughout growth, and that vascularity of the frontoparietal domes decreased with size.

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Schott and Evans concluded that variability in the number and shape of nodes on the squamosal shelf was due to individual variation rather than ontogeny.
facts.quote: A 2012 study by Schott and Evans found that the number and shape of the individual nodes on the squamosal shelf of the examined S. validum skulls varied considerably, and that this variability does not seem to correlate with ontogenic changes, but was due to individual variation.

facts.statement: The function of the Stegoceras dome is debated, with interpretations ranging from a weapon for intra-specific combat to a structure for sexual display or species recognition.
facts.quote: The function of pachycephalosaur domes has been debated, and Stegoceras has been used as a model for experimentation in various studies. The dome has mainly been interpreted as a weapon used in intra-specific combat, a sexual display structure, or a means for species recognition.

facts.statement: Palaeontologist Edwin Colbert first suggested in 1955 that Stegoceras domed skulls were used for head-butting.
facts.quote: The hypothesis that the domed skulls of Stegoceras and other pachycephalosaurs were used for butting heads was first suggested by palaeontologist Edwin Colbert in 1955.

facts.statement: Galton argued that the dome could function as a battering-ram if the skull was held vertically perpendicular to the neck to transmit force without dislocation.
facts.quote: Galton suggested that when Stegoceras held its skull vertically, perpendicular to the neck, force would be transmitted from the skull, with little chance of it being dislocated, and the dome could therefore be used as a battering-ram.

facts.statement: In 1978, Sues supported the head-butting hypothesis based on plexi-glass models showing the anatomy could transmit dome-to-dome impact stress.
facts.quote: In 1978, Sues agreed with Galton that the anatomy of pachycephalosaurs was consistent with transmitting dome-to-dome impact stress, based on tests with plexi-glass models.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter (1997) argued that the curved posture of the neck and back made horizontal head-butting physically impossible for Stegoceras.
facts.quote: In 1997, palaeontologist Kenneth Carpenter pointed out that the dorsal vertebrae from the back of the pachycephalosaur Homalocephale show that the back curved downwards just before the neck (which was not preserved), and unless the neck curved upwards, the head would point to the ground.

facts.statement: Carpenter proposed that Stegoceras used its dome for flank-butting, where animals stood parallel and struck the sides of opponents.
facts.quote: Because of the problems he found with the head-butting hypothesis, Carpenter instead suggested the domes were adaptations for flank-butting (as seen in some large African mammals); he imagined that two animals would stand parallel, facing each other or the same direction, and direct blows to the side of the opponent.

facts.statement: Carpenter suggested Stegoceras engaged in threat displays by bobbing heads to show dome size before delivering blows until one opponent submitted.
facts.quote: Carpenter suggested that the pachycephalosaurs would have first engaged in threat display by bobbing and presenting their heads to show the size of their domes (intimidation), and thereafter delivered blows to each other, until one opponent signalled submission.

facts.statement: Stegoceras possessed a skull shape similar to bighorn sheep, featuring cancellous bone that protected the brain.
facts.quote: Stegoceras and Prenocephale both had skull shapes similar to the bighorn sheep with cancellous bone protecting the brain.

facts.statement: The concentration of trauma lesions at the top of the dome supports the hypothesis that Stegoceras engaged in head-butting behavior.
facts.quote: The distribution of lesions in these animals tended to concentrate at the top of the dome, which supports head-butting behaviour.

facts.statement: Research indicates that while Stegoceras forelimb musculature was conservative compared to early bipedal saurischians, its pelvic and hindlimb musculature was more derived due to skeletal peculiarities.
facts.quote: They found that the musculature of the forelimbs was conservative, particularly compared to those of early bipedal saurischian dinosaurs, but the pelvic and hindlimb musculature was instead more derived, due to peculiarities of the skeleton.

facts.statement: In 1998, Goodwin and colleagues argued that the lack of sinuses and the honeycomb-like vascular bone structure made the dome ill-suited for head-butting, risking fractures in adjacent bones.
facts.quote: In 1998, Goodwin and colleagues considered the lack of sinuses in the skull of Stegoceras and the "honeycomb"-like network of vascular bone in the dome ill-suited for head-butting, and pointed out that the bones adjacent to the dome risked fracture during such contact.

facts.statement: A 2004 study by Goodwin and colleagues found that dome vascularity decreased with age, a pattern they argued was inconsistent with functions in head-butting or heat-exchange.
facts.quote: In 2004, Goodwin and colleagues studied the cranial histology of pachycephalosaurs, and found that the vascularity (including the trabeculae) of the domes decreased with age, which they found inconsistent with a function in either head-butting or heat-exchange.

facts.statement: In 2011, Padian and Horner proposed that bizarre dinosaur structures like domes were primarily for species recognition, dismissing other explanations as unsupported.
facts.quote: In 2011, palaeontologists Kevin Padian and John R. Horner proposed that "bizarre structures" in dinosaurs in general (including domes, frills, horns, and crests) were primarily used for species recognition, and dismissed other explanations as unsupported by evidence.

facts.statement: A 2023 study found that Stegoceras specimens varied in frontonasal boss thickness, with the tallest bosses showing the most bone pathologies, suggesting the variation represents intersexual differences.
facts.quote: Dyer and colleagues found in 2023 that Stegoceras specimens differed in the thickness of the frontonasal boss, and that skulls with the most bone pathologies were those with the tallest bosses, which they considered indication that variation in boss thickness represents intersexual variation.

facts.statement: Horner and colleagues stated in 2023 that the early development of domes and ornamentation in Stegoceras indicates they were used for visual communication to allow juveniles and adults to recognize one another.
facts.quote: In 2023, Horner and colleagues stated that since the dome and associated ornamentation of Stegoceras and the ornamentation of Pachycephalosaurus developed early in life, this indicates they were used for visual communication, so that juveniles could recognise other juveniles and adults other adults.

facts.statement: Stegoceras validum lived between 77.5 and 75 million years ago in Alberta, Canada, within the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations.
facts.quote: S. validum is known from the late Late Cretaceous Belly River Group (the Canadian equivalent to the Judith River Group in the US), and specimens have been recovered from the Dinosaur Park Formation (late Campanian, 76.5 to 75 mya) in Dinosaur Provincial Park (including the lectotype specimen), and the Oldman Formation (middle Campanian, 77.5 to 76.5 mya) of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: Stegoceras novomexicanum lived approximately 75 to 74 million years ago in New Mexico.
facts.quote: S. novomexicanum is known from the Fruitland (late Campanian, about 75 mya) and lower Kirtland Formation (late Campanian, about 74 mya) of New Mexico

facts.statement: The environment of the Dinosaur Park Formation was a low-relief landscape of rivers and floodplains that became increasingly swampy and influenced by marine conditions.
facts.quote: The Dinosaur Park Formation is interpreted as a low-relief setting of rivers and floodplains that became more swampy and influenced by marine conditions over time as the Western Interior Seaway transgressed westward.

facts.statement: The climate in the Dinosaur Park Formation was warmer than modern Alberta, lacking frost but featuring distinct wet and dry seasons.
facts.quote: The climate was warmer than present-day Alberta, without frost, but with wetter and drier seasons.

facts.statement: Conifers formed the dominant canopy, while ferns, tree ferns, and flowering plants made up the understory in the Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: Conifers were apparently the dominant canopy plants, with an understory of ferns, tree ferns, and angiosperms.

facts.quote: S. validum se conoce de la Formación Dinosaur Park y la Formación Oldman , mientras que S. novomexicanum es de la Formación Fruitland y Kirtland

facts.statement: The UALVP 2 specimen of S. validum is the most complete Stegoceras individual known to date.
facts.quote: El espécimen de S. validum UALVP 2 es el individuo de Stegoceras más completo conocido hasta la fecha

facts.statement: Its estimated length was approximately 2 to 2.5 meters, comparable to the size of a goat.
facts.quote: Se estima que su longitud fue de aproximadamente 2 a 2,5m, comparable al tamaño de una cabra

facts.statement: Its weight has been estimated at around 10 to 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: El peso se ha estimado en alrededor de 10 a 40kg

facts.statement: Stegoceras is one of the most known North American pachycephalosaurs and one of the few known from postcranial remains.
facts.quote: Stegoceras es uno de los paquicefalosáuridos norteamericanos más conocidos y uno de los pocos conocidos a partir de restos poscraneales

facts.statement: The frontal and parietal bones were very thick and formed an elevated dome.
facts.quote: Los huesos frontal y parietal eran muy gruesos y formaban una cúpula elevada

facts.statement: The suture between these two elements was obliterated, only slightly visible in some specimens, and they are collectively called "frontoparietals".
facts.quote: La sutura entre estos dos elementos se eliminó, solo ligeramente visible en algunos especímenes y se denominan colectivamente "frontoparietales"

facts.statement: The squamosal bone was large, did not form part of the dome, and the posterior part was swollen.
facts.quote: El escamoso era grande, no formaba parte de la cúpula, y la parte posterior estaba hinchada

facts.statement: It was adorned with irregularly spaced tubercles, and a row of nodules or protuberances extended along its upper edges, ending in a pointed tubercle or small horn on each side at the back of the skull.
facts.quote: Estaba adornado con tubérculos espaciados irregularmente y una fila de nódulos o protuberancias se extendía a lo largo de sus bordes superiores, terminando en un tubérculo puntiagudo o pequeño cuerno a cada lado en la parte posterior del cráneo

facts.statement: Except for the upper surface of the dome, most of the skull was adorned with nodules, many arranged in rows.
facts.quote: Excepto por la superficie superior de la cúpula, gran parte del cráneo estaba adornado con nódulos, muchos dispuestos en filas

facts.statement: The large orbit had the shape of an imperfect ellipse, with the longest axis from front to back, and was oriented to the side and slightly forward.
facts.quote: La gran órbita tenía la forma de una elipse imperfecta, con el eje más largo de adelante hacia atrás y estaba orientada hacia un lado y ligeramente hacia adelante

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone formed the lower front margin of the orbit, and its surface had rows of ornamentation in the shape of nodes.
facts.quote: El hueso lagrimal formaba el margen frontal inferior de la órbita, y su superficie tenía filas de ornamentación en forma de nodo

facts.statement: The prefrontal and palpebral bones were fused and formed a thick crest above the orbit.
facts.quote: Los huesos prefrontal y palpebral estaban fusionados y formaban una cresta gruesa por encima de la órbita

facts.statement: The relatively large jugal bone formed the lower margin of the orbit, extending far forward and downward toward the jaw joint.
facts.quote: El hueso yugal relativamente grande formaba el margen inferior de la órbita, extendiéndose mucho hacia adelante y hacia abajo, hacia la articulación de la mandíbula

facts.statement: The nasal openings were large and oriented toward the front.
facts.quote: Las aberturas nasales eran grandes y estaban orientadas hacia el frente

facts.statement: The nasal bone was thick, strongly sculpted, and had a convex profile.
facts.quote: El hueso nasal era grueso, fuertemente esculpido y tenía un perfil convexo

facts.statement: There was a small foramen in the suture between the premaxillae that led to the nasal cavity and was possibly connected to the Jacobson organ, a sense of smell organ.
facts.quote: Había un pequeño foramen en la sutura entre los premaxilares, que conducía a la cavidad nasal y posiblemente estaba conectado al órgano de Jacobson, un órgano del sentido del olfato

facts.statement: Stegoceras had teeth that were heterodont, different from each other, and thecodont, placed in alveoli.
facts.quote: Stegoceras tenía dientes que eran heterodontes, diferentes entre sí, y tecodontes, colocados en alvéolos

facts.statement: On each side, the most complete specimen, UALVP 2, had three teeth in the premaxilla, sixteen in the maxilla (both part of the upper jaw), and seventeen in the dentary of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: De cada lado, el ejemplar más completo, UALVP 2, tenía tres dientes en el premaxilar, dieciséis en el maxilar, ambos parte del maxilar superior, y diecisiete en el dentario del maxilar inferior

facts.statement: The premaxillary teeth were separated from those behind the maxilla by a small diastema (space), and the two rows in the premaxilla were separated by a toothless space at the front.
facts.quote: Los dientes del premaxilar estaban separados de los que estaban detrás del maxilar por una pequeña diastema, espacio, y las dos filas en el premaxilar estaban separadas por un espacio desdentado en el frente

facts.statement: The front teeth of the lower maxilla were larger than those of the upper maxilla.
facts.quote: Los dientes frontales del maxilar inferior eran más grandes que los del maxilar superior

facts.statement: The front edges of the crowns had eight denticles, and the rear edge had nine to eleven.
facts.quote: Los bordes delanteros de las coronas tenían ocho dentículos y el borde trasero tenía de nueve a once

facts.statement: The teeth in the rear of the upper jaw, maxilla, and lower jaw were triangular in lateral view and compressed in frontal view.
facts.quote: Los dientes en la parte posterior de la mandíbula superior, el maxilar, e inferior eran triangulares en vista lateral y comprimidos en vista frontal

facts.statement: The skull of Stegoceras is distinguished by a prominent parieto-squamosal projection that became smaller with age, an incipient frontal parietal dome that increased in size with age, inflated nasal bones, and ornamentation of tubercles on the sides and tops of the squamosal bones.
facts.quote: El cráneo de Stegoceras se puede distinguir de los de otros paquicefalosáuridos por características tales como su saliente parietoescamosal pronunciada, aunque se hizo más pequeño con la edad, la cúpula "incipiente" de su frontoparental, aunque la cúpula aumentó con la edad, sus huesos nasales inflados, su ornamentación de tubérculos en los costados y dorso de los huesos escamosos, hileras de hasta seis tubérculos en la cara superior de cada escamoso, y hasta dos nódulos en la retroproyección del parietal.

facts.statement: The incomplete vertebral column of Stegoceras appears to have been very rigid due to articulations between zygapophyses that prevented lateral movement, further strengthened by ossified tendons.
facts.quote: La columna vertebral de Stegoceras se conoce de forma incompleta. La articulación entre las cigofisis, procesos articulares, de las vértebras dorsales de la espalda posterior sucesivas parece haber impedido el movimiento lateral de la columna vertebral, lo que la hizo muy rígida, y fue fortalecida aún más por los tendones osificados.

facts.statement: Based on its position in Homalocephale, ossified tendons found with UALVP2 likely formed an intricate "caudal basket" in the tail consisting of parallel rows where the ends of each tendon contacted the next successively.
facts.quote: Basado en su posición en Homalocephale, los tendones osificados encontrados con UALVP2 habrían formado una intrincada "canasta caudal" en la cola, que consiste en filas paralelas, con los extremos de cada tendón en contacto con el siguiente sucesivamente.

facts.statement: The femur was thin and curved inward, the tibia was thin and twisted, and the fibula was thin and wide at the upper end.
facts.quote: El fémur, hueso del muslo, era delgado y curvado hacia adentro, la tibia era delgada y torcida, y el peroné era delgado y ancho en el extremo superior.

facts.statement: The first known remains of Stegoceras were collected by Canadian paleontologist Lawrence Lambe from the Belly River Group in the Red Deer River district of Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos conocidos de Stegoceras fueron recolectados por el paleontólogo canadiense Lawrence Lambe del Grupo Belly River, en el distrito Río Red Deer de Alberta, Canadá.

facts.statement: Based on these specimens, Lambe described and named the new monotypic genus and species Stegoceras validum in 1902.
facts.quote: Con base en estos especímenes, Lambe describió y denominó al nuevo género y especie monotípica Stegoceras validus en 1902.

facts.statement: The generic name Stegoceras comes from the Greek stegè, meaning "roof", and keras, meaning "horn".
facts.quote: El nombre genérico `Stegoceras proviene del griego stegè, στέγη, que significa "techo" y keras, κέρας, que significa "cuerno".

facts.statement: The specific name S. validus means "strong" in Latin, possibly referring to the thick roof of the skull.
facts.quote: El nombre específico S. validus significa "fuerte" en latín, posiblemente en referencia al grueso techo del cráneo.

facts.statement: Stegoceras belongs to the parent group Eupachycephalosauria.
facts.quote: Parent group: Eupachycephalosauria

facts.statement: Stegoceras is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Stegoceras lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)
